n: Isaiah addresses a land “beyond the rivers of Ethiopia” — most scholars think of Cush (Nubia), whose kings then ruled Egypt and sought allies against Assyria. Some Latter-day Saint readers have also seen a latter-day land in this verse, but its meaning is debated.

f.g: Possibly “Ho!” or “Ah!” — a call for attention rather than a curse.
Possibly “whirring wings,” referring to insects of the Nile region, or to the land’s protecting outreach.
Hebrew Cush — the region south of Egypt (modern Sudan).

n: This land sends envoys by sea in papyrus boats. Isaiah tells the swift messengers to return to their tall, smooth-skinned people, feared far and wide, a strong nation whose land is divided by rivers.

f.g: Light papyrus boats used on the Nile.

n: All people of the world are told to watch for God’s banner raised on the mountains and listen for His trumpet. The Lord, not human alliances, controls events.
The Lord says He will quietly watch from His dwelling, like shimmering heat in sunshine or a cloud of dew in harvest time — calm, patient, and in control.

f.g: I will stay quiet and watch.

n: Then, just before harvest, when the grapes are forming, He will cut off the shoots and branches. He will strike at the right moment — likely referring to Assyria’s sudden defeat.
The pruned branches — fallen enemy soldiers — will be left for birds and wild animals through summer and winter.
Then this same distant, mighty people will bring gifts to the Lord at Mount Zion. Even far nations will one day honor Israel’s God.

f.w: the present be brought unto the LORD of hosts
the place of the name of the LORD
